items.originalTitle: Scott Olson—Getty Images
items.author: Chad de Guzman
items.title: Scott Olson—Getty Images
items.summary: A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 19, 2026. The U.S. Army said it is pushing through with the controlled detonation of more than five dozen barrels of a toxic explosive chemical in an Iowa munitions plant on Wednesday, despite public outcry over the potential health impacts on neighboring communities and an ongoing legal battle. Nearly five tons of degraded lead azide, a chemical compound used as a detonator in cartridges and shells, are set to be detonated at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a city in Des Moines County of nearly 400 people some 13 km away from the Mississippi River separating the state from Illinois. On Nov. 19, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle posted on social media that discussions with environmental officials and the local community determined a controlled detonation of the lead azide stockpile “posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area,” but he announced that the detonation would be postponed from Nov. 20 to Nov. 23. Also on Nov. 19, environmental groups sued the Environmental Protection Agency, which granted the permit to the U.S. Army to carry out the detonation, and a federal appeals court ordered a temporary freeze on the permit. Then, on Nov. 21, the Justice Department said it plans to use emergency powers to avoid the permit requirement for detonation. On Nov. 22, the Army rescheduled the blast for Nov. 25, saying that the new time would “allow for more optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced.” Environmental groups have argued that the U.S. Army is “ sidestepping ” the judicial process. They claim that the EPA approved the detonation plan without enough public notice and without thoroughly studying alternatives. The detonation risks community exposure to lead, a neurotoxin health officials have long documented to cause a variety of health problems in pregnant women and children. There is no safe exposure level to lead: exposed children can suffer damage to the brain and nervous system, learning and behavioral issues, speech and hearing impairments, while pregnant women face increased risks of premature births and miscarriages. The Federal Aviation Administration has restricted flights around Middletown from Monday through Wednesday. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds activated a state emergency operations center on Nov. 20. In neighboring Illinois, officials argued that they are similarly at risk from airborne lead-containing particles the detonation will produce. On Sunday, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said he spoke with the Army, the EPA, and other agencies about the planned detonation, adding that he was “continuing to press for the release of more public information to help keep Illinoisans safe.” “The Army has clearly mishandled this situation, and Iowans and residents in our neighboring states deserve a full review of all of the missteps that led us to this point,” said Wally Taylor, attorney for the environmental organization Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter, one of the petitioners against the EPA. “However, if detonation is now the only option, it is imperative that everyone impacted has access to the full range of testing, mitigation, and remediation resources.” Why is the Army choosing to detonate the stockpile? In March, during what the Army said was a “routine stockpile surveillance operation” at the 19,000-acre plant, technicians discovered 68 drums of degraded lead azide in underground concrete bunkers, which it said had potentially become unstable. The barrels have languished underground for nearly two decades, and the Army said moving the chemical off-site for disposal would risk accidental detonation. Between April and September 2026, the EPA issued three emergency storage permits so the Army could continue storing the stockpile safely while the Army assessed how to treat it. In its environmental assessment , the Army concluded that doing nothing would create “a constant threat of an accidental, unmitigated detonation,” which would have “significant, uncontrolled adverse impacts.” But while detonating the stockpile on-site would “produce severe, instantaneous physical effects” such as blast overpressure and noise and would locally release hazardous materials such as lead particulates and combustion gases in the short term, the Army says these impacts are “heavily mitigated.” Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist for the Army Sustainment Command, told a local news station on Nov. 18 that the Army’s window to safely dispose of the stockpiles was narrowing as winter is arriving. Barati said colder weather or disturbances could cause the stockpiles to detonate spontaneously. “We’re trying to do a controlled detonation to minimize the impact to the community and the environment,” Barati said. “This is not something that we take lightly. We know that this is a disruption to people and that is not our intent, but we’re trying to do this in the safest manner possible.” On Nov. 21, the New York Times reported that, in late March, the Army had initially awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based company that would neutralize the stockpile using chemicals. But two months later, it canceled the deal over purported safety concerns. The EPA granted an emergency permit to detonate the stockpiles between Nov. 13, 2026 and Feb. 11, 2027. The permit for the on-site detonation echoed the risk linked with alternative means of disposal, saying that “recrystallization of the lead azide during long-term storage has increased the material’s sensitivity to friction and shock, creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation.” In the Army’s public notice issued just days before the initial blast schedule , it said the lead azide barrels will be detonated in two, rapid-fire shots inside concrete, earth-covered magazines surrounded by Hesco barriers filled with sand about two stories high. Before and during the detonation, the soil above the magazines will be saturated with water, and water misters will be spraying, all in an attempt to control the amount of lead that could travel through the air beyond the plant. The notice added that models projected the level of lead particles in the air after the detonation “may be elevated but well below the level at which EPA would require protective actions be taken.” What’s the legal battle about? Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club, both nonprofit environmental advocacy organizations, sought to suspend the EPA permit. In a suit filed before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit, the plaintiffs argued that the permit authorized the Army to detonate the lead azide “in the open,” adding that the blast would create “a plume of lead dust that will blanket homes and communities” possibly as far as 100 mi or more. The petitioners argued that the Army did not promptly and accurately inform the public of the detonation and its impact. The Army said it had informed the local community ahead of the planned blast, including at an open house at the Army Reserve Center in mid-October, but the petitioners argued many residents and local officials claimed to only have learned of the planned detonation “through friends and social media.” The petitioners also emphasized how there’s no safe level of exposure to lead. The court sided with the petitioners and granted the emergency stay on Nov. 19 pending the ruling. But in its Nov. 21 filing to the court, the Justice Department said it would use emergency powers allowing the Army to continue with the blast without an environmental permit, citing federal exemptions. The department emphasized the “immediate risk” posed by the stockpile, while saying that the Army “intends to act consistent with the terms of the Emergency Permit and its mitigation measures even if not in effect.” Thien Chau, an attorney for Earthjustice, which helped sue the EPA, said in a statement that “despite claiming public safety is its top priority and public communication is essential to trust, the Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm.” What’s the anticipated impact of the detonation? While safety measures will be fully enforced, the Army said in its public notice that during the detonation, it anticipates ground vibration and a dust plume that spreads “some lead-containing particles” in the air, which will deposit on the ground. The notice said Middletown residents can expect the plume to linger for no more than an hour, depending on wind speed. The Army advised residents to evacuate and avoid the affected area in Iowa, and urged those who could not leave to stay indoors, close windows and doors, and turn off heating and ​cooling systems that could bring in outside air. It also said residents should wet-clean surfaces to remove lead dust. Precautionary measures were not limited to Iowa: In Illinois, agriculture officials recommended ways to protect livestock and pets, including keeping animals indoors until the plume passes, and their rigorous washing afterward. Amid this, several politicians continued to express concern over the risks ahead of the continued detonation. U.S. Senator-elect Josh Turek of Iowa posted on social media Sunday that he believes that a full investigation is needed not only into the stockpile’s prolonged unsafe treatment and why safer methods of disposal are needed, but also into “what other potentially dangerous materials are being stored at [the plant] and their condition, and what procedures are needed to ensure this never happens again.” Turek as well as a group of Illinois Democrats—U.S. Senators Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth; Lieutenant Governor and U.S. Senator-elect Juliana Stratton; U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen; and Gov. Pritzker—and two Illinois Republicans, Representatives Darin LaHood and Mary Miller, sent a letter to acting Army Secretary Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin on Nov. 19 expressing their grave concerns over the planned detonation, calling to postpone it. The potential health risk caused by the detonation threatens Iowa, which is already suffering from having one of the highest cancer incidences in the U.S. “Because of the decisions that have already been made over the course of months, if not years, no good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been,” Rob Sand, who’s set to take office as Iowa’s new governor in January, posted Sunday. “Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again.”

The problem is, she’s already engaged to another. Akeem hides his identity as a royal prince and works at her father’s fast-food restaurant to get closer to her. Will Akeem and Lisa fall in love as he cosplays being working class. Will Lisa leave her rich but arrogant fiance? Will their families accept their Lisa and Akeem if they do decide to marry? items.title: The Right’s Absurd Misreading of Orwell
items.summary: “Orwell Saw This Coming” ran the headline, and if you didn’t read any further, you might agree. The president was whipping up hatred in elaborate rage-fueled rallies and plastering banners bearing his glowering, oversize face on government buildings. The National Guard was patrolling the streets of Washington. Officials in the recently renamed Department of War were bragging about extrajudicial killings. The national-security apparatus had divided the world into three zones of influence, strikingly similar to The Party’s Oceania, Eurasia, and Eastasia from 1984 . But none of that was the this in “Orwell Saw This Coming,” which ran in The Free Press in January. This was New York City’s new mayor. “It’s fair to say that George Orwell would have despised Zohran Mamdani,” the columnist Charles Lane argued. Trump was hardly mentioned. In 2026, if an American writer brings up Orwell, chances are high that their target is the left, not the right. Over the past decade, one of the strangest habits among right-wing intellectuals and pundits has been their use of Orwell to defend the rise of authoritarianism in the U.S. The reference is shockingly common . “If 1984 has a practical lesson, it is this: There is a world of difference between a despotism dedicated to the expansion of socialism through federal-government power and a despotism dedicated to dismantling it,” Nathan Schlueter wrote in 2017 in National Review . “The former suffocates; the latter, though not without its serious dangers, just might create room to breathe.” The most direct rebuttal to this absurdity is Orwell’s own: “My recent novel is NOT intended as an attack on Socialism or on the British Labour Party (of which I am a supporter)” he once wrote to a curious reader. Orwell was literally antifa. In Spain, he fought with the militia of the Workers’ Party of Marxist Unification. Barcelona has a square named after him, and not because he supported far-right authoritarians against academics and students, as many conservative intellectuals would seem to believe. [ From the May 2024 issue: What Orwell really feared ] Let’s call them the Orwellian Trumpists. They could not have misunderstood the writer, or the current political reality, any more thoroughly. To a certain extent, Orwell saw this coming. The dumbest mistakes are typically made by the intelligentsia, he once cautioned: “No ordinary man could be such a fool.” He has now become the subject of his own warning. Orwell transcends right and left in this sense: Everyone who writes a political opinion in English, whatever their persuasion, is following in his tradition. “Why I Write” and “Politics and the English Language” are the foundational texts of magazine and newspaper writing to this day. His style is so hard to replicate because it is so basic. Reading Orwell is like hearing a man say what he means. It’s an astonishingly difficult effect to imitate. I’m trying to write like him now. Almost every opinion writer you can name is trying to write like him too. The roots of right-wing Orwell worship are not hard to see when you consider his obsession with prose style and the debasement of political language. Orwell believed in political writing more than any other writer; he gave it a grandeur and a sense of purpose that play to the vanities of every opinion columnist. He believed in clarity, not just freedom of speech. Staleness, imprecision, and pretension were, for him, far more than technical flaws. They were signs of the onset of dehumanization. Over the past decade, as the banalities of identity politics entered academia and journalism, Orwell became an ideal lens by which to witness and critique the process. The left’s attempt to impose a new linguistic order by force of shame was, in fact, an attempt to repress the human. But the problem with today’s right-wing Orwellians is that they are living in the past. Trumpism is a far greater threat to the values Orwell fought for than wokeness ever could be. “The Orwellian Big Brother punishing you for expressing an impolitic thought is now the law of the land in the land of Orwell,” Rupa Subramanya, another writer for The Free Press , told a congressional committee last year. She said this while the Republican Party was detaining students for signing op-eds, and policing the border by looking for inappropriate social-media posts. DOGE, meanwhile, was pulling funding from government agencies on the basis of keyword searches. Everyone who has ever argued that the most significant threat to the Western canon comes from the left will need to reckon with the fact that Republicans were the ones who told professors to pull passages from Plato from a course at Texas A&M. It was Republicans who threw CDC data sets and significant chunks of the National Archives into a memory hole. Trump’s decrees about language have gone further than any Democrat ever dared: He changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Lake Ontario, to his obedient followers, is Lake America. The Orwellian Trumpists’ claims to support linguistic freedom are laughable, or beside the point. In their bitter partisanship, they resemble the neoconservatives of a previous era, the liberals mugged by reality. They lack the dignity of their predecessors, though. They’ve been mugged by reality television. I think of them as the Otto intellectuals: Otto is the character from the 1980s British comedy A Fish Called Wanda who thinks that Aristotle was Belgian and that the central message of Buddhism is every man for himself. The contortions of the Orwellian Trumpists would dazzle any Soviet apparatchik. The British historian Niall Ferguson, who has used Orwell’s line that “to see what is in front of one’s nose needs a constant struggle” on multiple occasions, has frequently sane-washed Trump’s foreign policy. In an episode of the Hoover Institution’s podcast GoodFellows about Trump’s “coercive diplomacy,” Ferguson claimed that Trump’s destruction of America’s alliances and his sprawling, pointless violence were the result of deep strategic thinking. If you’re arguing in favor of “coercive diplomacy,” a phrase precisely as meaningful as “violent seduction,” you’re not George Orwell. You’re closer to Lord Haw Haw. Sometimes, as with the right-wing activist Christopher Rufo, using Orwell has explicitly partisan purposes. “What happens is that the left will say, ‘Well you’re opposing DEI; you don’t like diversity, you don’t like equity, you don’t like inclusion,’” Rufo said on his YouTube channel. “And you can say no, those are false words, those are Orwellian terms.” Citing Orwell becomes a technique in such cases, although aimed at a negligible slice of the political sphere: people who have heard the word Orwellian but have never bothered to think through what it means. [ Thomas Chatterton Williams: The right is changing the rules of the culture war ] As Orwell wrote in “Politics and the English Language,” he hated any argument that “consists in gumming together long strips of words which have already been set in order by someone else, and making the results presentable by sheer humbug.” Orwell has become what he most despised. He has set the strips of words in order, and someone else is gumming them together by sheer humbug. He’s jargon now. He’s the jargon for the supposedly anti-jargon crowd. Orwell’s contradictory status reminds me of his magnificent essay on Charles Dickens. Orwell is as distant from us today as Dickens was from Orwell. He was trying to understand how Dickens could be appropriated by people he would obviously have despised. “Dickens attacked English institutions with a ferocity that has never since been approached,” Orwell wrote. “Yet he managed to do it without making himself hated, and, more than this, the very people he attacked have swallowed him so completely that he has become a national institution himself.” The audience remembered his sentimentality. The actual import of his writing vanished. Dickens was critical of virtually every entrenched system in English life but even more critical of the attempts to overturn those systems. Tradition was brutality; revolution was terror. Dickens walked a line between “attacking everybody and antagonizing nobody,” Orwell wrote. In the end, Orwell could not suppress his adulation for the contradiction, for the refusal to fit: Dickens was “a type hated with equal hatred by all the smelly little orthodoxies which are now contending for our souls,” he wrote. Those orthodoxies, unable to face Dickens’s recognition of their own fraudulence but unable to reject him because of the power of his writing, turned him into a vibe. The Dickens vibe remains in place today: squalid London, Christmas, cheekiness, wretched children. Orwell is being turned into a vibe just as Dickens before him. He is English to the fingertips: late-imperial, pre-multicultural, pubs with barmaids who call you “dearie,” memorized passages of Kipling, bad food, warm beer, and floggings in public schools—combined with a staunch criticism of every bit of that. Orwell was an Eton graduate who nonetheless described the upper classes as drunken, violent buffoons who were tolerable only at the moment they were being shot. At the same time, he was a committed leftist who became a critic of the totalitarian left as it took power across various states in the middle of the 20th century. The Orwell vibe is “aren’t English people clever?” meets “internal critic of the left.” As with Dickens, the vibe is half correct, half oblivious. The reason Orwell is such a paragon—the reason you can still feel the power of his writing long after every politician he mentioned is dead—is that he remained a party of one, even when he was shooting people or elephants, even when highly civilized human beings were flying overhead , trying to kill him. Now he exists through his contradictions: an Englishman who saw the brutality of England and yet remained English, a leftist who faced the brutality of Communism and yet remained a leftist. “The words of a dead man are modified in the guts of the living,” as W. H. Auden said about Yeats. You can do what you like with Orwell’s words now. The Orwellian Trumpists have used their purported idol to justify a president who demands his followers accept obvious lies, who runs the government according to a standard of personal loyalty, who campaigns on two-minute hate, who revels in suspending the rules of war, who tears children from their mothers, who pardons for a fee, who has done everything in his power to separate language from meaning in order to camouflage his own brutality. They find themselves in an untenable position: Either they wanted all this or they have to admit that they got suckered by the most obvious con man in the history of con men. Perhaps it was inevitable that Orwell would devolve into just another vibe. But it’s shameful what that vibe turned out to be; the Orwellian Trumpists have chosen a boot stamping on a human face. It remains true that to see what’s in front of one’s nose requires a constant struggle.

items.title: How the Blue Wave Missed Florida
items.summary: When the midterms’ blue wave hit the southern United States a few weeks ago, one conspicuous red patch remained: Florida. There, unlike in nearby Georgia and Texas, Democrats running for senator and governor both lost their races—narrowly, but still. Much of the explanation for Florida’s enduring redness is that the state has absorbed hundreds of thousands of newcomers in recent years, and these individuals largely moved to Florida in order to be Republican . Starting in 2020, Florida became a magnet for Republicans from other states who yearned for a place with conservative politics and a relatively low cost of living. Research shows that people who moved to the state from around the country during the past six years were much more likely to register as Republicans than Democrats. And this month, many of these new arrivals voted to support the Republican policies that they’d relocated to enjoy. As the Republican senator Ashley Moody said in her victory speech on Election Night, many of the newcomers she met during her campaign “were desperate to hold on to what we have built here in this state.” For many years, Florida was a quintessential battleground. Liberal retirees largely settled on the state’s east coast, in solidly blue Miami-Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach Counties, while conservative retirees flocked to the panhandle and parts of the Gulf Coast. The state’s Democrats and Republicans largely balanced each other out: George W. Bush eked out a victory in 2000 in part by the grace of hanging chads , then won handily in 2004. Barack Obama won the state in 2008 and 2012; in 2016, Donald Trump beat Hillary Clinton by just over 100,000 votes. In 2018 , Democrats outnumbered Republicans in Florida by more than 200,000 registered voters. [ Read: Why people won’t stop moving to the Sun Belt ] Then came COVID. Many blue states had mask mandates, vaccine mandates, and prolonged school closures. Several of them placed new restrictions on policing after George Floyd’s murder or required the teaching of LGBTQ issues in public-school classrooms. Governor Ron DeSantis seized the opportunity to advertise Florida as a warm refuge from the cold winds of wokeness. He offered police officers a financial reward if they moved there from another state. He proclaimed the rise of the “free state of Florida”—even adding the line to highway welcome signs . “Occasionally you come across a tagline that really sticks, and that one did,” Susan MacManus, a political scientist at the University of South Florida, told me. The state’s lack of vaccine mandates, its aggressive school-reopening approach, and restrictions on teaching about sexual orientation were popular with right-leaning parents. So were the lack of state income tax and the prospect of going to the beach in February. A recent study by Daniel Smith, a political scientist at the University of Florida, and his colleagues found that, starting in 2020, the people who moved to Florida were much more likely to register on arrival as Republican than Democrat. Smith found that registered Republicans overall have lived in Florida a shorter amount of time than Democrats, and Democrats and independents from the Northeast are coming to Florida in much smaller numbers than they used to. By the beginning of this year, Florida had about 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats. Republican candidates in Florida had other advantages in the midterms, too. Byron Donalds raised more than six times as much money for his gubernatorial campaign as his Democratic rival, David Jolly. And the state’s Hispanic population might have been especially receptive to attacks on Democrats. “Trump and then other Republicans really labeled the Democrats successfully as socialists,” Aubrey Jewett, a political scientist at the University of Central Florida, told me. That might have turned Cuban Floridians, many of whom had negative experiences with that country’s socialist government, away from any candidate even notionally associated with democratic socialism—such as Angie Nixon, Moody’s Democratic rival for the Senate. But experts I spoke with nevertheless said that migration from other states helped push Republicans over the top. Especially with remote work an option for large numbers of white-collar workers, Jewett said, “we have imported hundreds of thousands of Republicans over the last five years.” Paul Chabot, the CEO of GOP Agent, a real-estate company that connects people with conservative Realtors, told me that on top of good weather and a low cost of living, his clients “are looking at pro-gun-friendly states.” They don’t want to live in a state with “a George Soros–funded” district attorney, he added, “because they feel like they won’t be safe there.” So they come to Florida, where Governor-Elect Donalds has an A+ rating from the National Rifle Association and three-quarters of the state’s elected prosecutors are Republican. To understand the distinctiveness of this Republican influx, consider Florida alongside Texas, a historically red state that saw a blue wave in the midterms. Like Florida, Texas welcomed hundreds of thousands of migrants from other states from 2020 to 2026. But research has shown that newcomers to Texas were more evenly divided among Democrats, Republicans, and the unaffiliated, and have not affected the state’s partisan balance by much. The “majority of the people who are moving to Texas from other states are doing it for economic reasons or family reasons,” Mark P. Jones, a political scientist at Rice University, told me. [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] Texas has seen some “political refugees” from California and other liberal states who do vote overwhelmingly Republican, Jones said. But left-leaning economic migrants seem to have arrived in larger numbers, and when many of them settled around Austin for tech jobs, they turned some of its surrounding counties blue, Jones said. In recent years, the state’s Republican politicians—three of whom had been in office for more than 10 years—were not popular, he added, and moderate Republican voters began to see Democrats as more palatable. Texas is still pink, Jones said—not quite purple. But, he said, “even a pink state can’t withstand an exceptionally unpopular president, a deeply flawed U.S. Senate candidate ,” and “a moribund economy that Republicans essentially hold all the responsibility for.” Whether Florida will continue on as a red state or shift back toward purple is unclear. Migration to the Sunshine State is slowing for a number of reasons. Some companies are calling remote workers back to the office, meaning that fewer people have the option to move wherever they wish. Plus, now that the COVID era is over, DeSantis is about to be out of office, and even some Democrats are disavowing the excesses of “ Woke 1 ,” the “free state of Florida” might not beckon the way it once did. Without a steady flow of conservative arrivals, the state could start tilting back to the center—or eventually to the left. People who were born in Florida are much less likely to be Republican than newcomers are, Smith said. And young voters, who are likelier to be Democrats, will eventually replace the state’s Baby Boomers as the latter go to that great beach house in the sky. Florida Democrats did notch some wins in the midterms: Pia Dandiya picked up a Florida House seat that “Republicans thought for sure they were going to win,” Smith said. Palm Beach County—home of Mar-a-Lago—went for both Jolly and Nixon in significant numbers. Many likely thought Texas was safely Republican too, until it wasn’t. Another definition of free , after all, is “up for grabs.”

items.author: Ruth Gilligan
items.title: Adder Stone by Clare Clark review – the story of a drowned Welsh village
items.summary: A real-life flooding becomes a flashpoint in this novel exploring family relationships, female liberation and the drive for Welsh independence In the author’s note accompanying her eighth novel, Adder Stone, Clare Clark recalls first learning how a lake in the Welsh valleys shrank during the drought of 1976 only to reveal an abandoned village underneath. As a child, Clark became obsessed with the idea, envisaging a sort of Welsh Pompeii – houses and lives frozen in time, buried beneath the water and the mud. Fifty years since that uncanny occurrence, Clark’s richly researched novel seeks to tell the story of that forgotten Welsh village: not abandoned by choice, but forcibly evicted in order to make way for a new reservoir needed to service Liverpool’s growing population. Clark charts how this event had a profound impact on individual lives, but also how it served as a flashpoint in the broader conversation around Welsh independence.

items.originalTitle: An Ode to Executive Assistants
items.author: 20th Century Fox / Everett Collection
items.title: An Ode to Executive Assistants
items.summary: T he executive assistants are being laid off. According to Bloomberg , firms such as PwC and McKinsey have cut thousands of assistant and other support-staff positions. From the start of 2023 until the summer of 2025, openings for entry-level jobs typically requiring at least some college dropped by 35 percent . What executive needs a 23-year-old with student loans and big dreams when they can use a personal AI assistant to manage their calendars and book their flights for free? You might think that this position is a perfect candidate for robot replacement. If AI can do mindless administrative tasks as well as any human, then all that’s left is the emotional labor, which can be heavy—managing the hyperspecific preferences and enormous egos of entitled corporate titans. Get rid of this position, and businesses would save money while young people would—perhaps—find less humiliating jobs. But I spent almost two years as an executive assistant, and one of the many things I learned was that no one—not even the bosses who might want to replace us—had any sense of what we actually did. These positions play an important role in the job market, providing a rare entry point into competitive fields. Executive assistants run last-minute errands. They steer their bosses away from annoying people at dinner parties and memorize faces and relationship histories. They know their boss’s intimate secrets and how to anticipate their needs. They put out fires before the boss smells smoke. They serve as office managers, nannies, baristas, and human encyclopedias. The better an assistant is at their job, in other words, the less anyone knows what they do all day. And when they’re gone, we’re really going to miss them. I f you ask executive assistants what they think about being replaced by AI, they might say that they welcome a robot taking over chores like filing expenses, but that they can’t imagine handing over the trickier parts of their job. Maguire Grace Amundsen was Kylie Jenner’s executive assistant for more than two years. She’s now a sort of girlboss influencer, and is starting an interview series with high-powered women called Hot Commodities . Being a good executive assistant, she told me, requires understanding “a lot that is not said.” You have to know “the person that you’re working for in a way where even if they don’t say something, you kind of know what they’re saying.” You have to understand their every mood. One woman, who used to be an executive assistant to a famous fashion designer and his chief marketing officer, and asked to remain anonymous because she had signed an NDA, said that if the designer “was in a good mood, it’s fine to send the email asking if it’s okay that the car is not a Range Rover for Friday. But if he’s in a terrible mood, sending that is literally going to kill your day.” “AI can’t predict all that,” she told me. Companies would need to “hire a human assistant to handle the AI assistant.” [ Sophie Gilbert: The Assistant and the messes women clean up ] Samantha, another former executive assistant, who asked me to use only her first name because she also signed an NDA, said that one of her most important roles was to serve as the scapegoat when anything went awry. She worked in the finance industry, and said a lot of her job was “taking the sword, and not taking that personally.” If something goes wrong anywhere in the company, you may be the one your boss yells at, and you get used to taking ownership for mistakes that weren’t your own. Samantha said she was privy to some of “the most intimate and personal things” in her bosses’ life: “colonoscopies, bonus sizes, who’s getting fired, who’s getting promoted, is divorce on the table.” The fashion assistant told me that the CMO’s “husband would call me. I talked to her driver. I talked to her hair stylist. I talked to her facialist. I talked to her kids. I talked to their school teachers.” At a time when most Americans distrust AI , it’s hard to imagine high-profile individuals wanting to share this kind of private information with a bot. But the more an executive assistant knows their boss, the more proactive they can be. High-powered executives often don’t have time to give instructions, and their assistants have to make judgment calls. “AI is really great at doing what you tell it to do, but a really good executive assistant is constantly thinking 345 steps ahead,” Samantha told me. “An EA needs to have the capacity to handle situations that don’t come with a clear set of instructions, whereas AI will always need a clear set of instructions.” Even if an executive theoretically fed an AI chatbot every bit of information (a big ask for someone who hires someone else to send their emails), there’s a level of nuance and emotional intelligence that you don’t get unless you are physically present in the room. Plus, most executives are looking to spend less time on their devices, not more. One of the main things assistants do is figure out what their boss actually needs to know from the onslaught of digital notifications and noise. “If you’re good at your job, you do a really great job of filtering, and I think that element would be lost,” Amundsen told me. To be fair, if you ask most anyone in most any field whether they think they can be replaced by AI, they’re likely to say absolutely not . But executive assistants have one more thing going for them: Perhaps the biggest reason executives like having them around is simply to flaunt them. “There is a level of prestige to having a dedicated assistant,” Anthony Taylor, an executive assistant at Hermès, told me. It’s how you know you’ve succeeded. He used to work at a smaller agency, where his old boss would bring him to events just to show that she was important enough to bring him to events. It’s the same reason that people send emails “looping my assistant in.” [ Annie Lowrey: How ChatGPT will destabilize white-collar work ] “No one’s going to be impressed by the fact that you’re paying some subsidiary of Claude to manage your calendar and your emails,” Taylor said. For this reason, human assistants will probably continue to have a place in status-obsessed industries that want to signal their refined taste, if nowhere else. These assistants don’t just book cars; they make sure the driver is wearing the right outfit and carrying the right brand of mints. They don’t just book the restaurant; they book the impossible restaurant, the kind you can’t get into unless someone at the hospitality group that owns the whole establishment owes you a favor. They cultivate their own network of maître d’s and publicists, and when their boss brings them to an event, they’re a status symbol in flesh and blood. T ake away the assistants , and lots of executives would probably have meltdowns. But that’s not what worries me most. The position of executive assistant is especially valuable for young people with backgrounds like mine. I would probably not be writing for this magazine if I hadn’t landed a job as an executive assistant here in 2023. I came from the South, had no connections in journalism, and little experience in the field. What I did have was a master’s degree, a résumé full of odd jobs, and the willingness to take notes in meetings. Eventually, I elbowed my way off the business side of the magazine and into writing. My story is a common one for people who want to land jobs in competitive, creative industries, but don’t have the perfect résumé or connections. “I was very unequipped, network-wise, moving to the city and pursuing fashion in any capacity, especially fashion PR, which is notoriously insular and elitist,” Taylor, who was raised in Mississippi, told me. When Taylor, who’s now 25, first set out to move to New York, he scoured the internet for anyone who could help him get his foot in the door. “My first actual successful attempt at networking was I strategically went on a date with someone who I knew worked in the industry,” he told me. It worked—his résumé was sent to a few agencies. He got an unpaid internship for a few months, during which he “spent all of my savings trying to stay afloat.” Eventually, a communications-assistant position that involved working on brand accounts opened up. He applied, but the role was given to the daughter of an executive at a major fashion magazine. The executive-assistant job was his “consolation prize,” he said. It required humility, but it was his ticket into the industry. Some people say that everyone should have to work a service-industry job, because there are certain life lessons that can only be learned as a 19-year-old bussing tables for snobby customers. My version of this argument is that everyone in corporate America should have to work as an assistant in their industry for a year. There are few jobs as frustrating and formative. You will learn to earn your keep. And if you’re as lucky as I was, you gain generous mentors who have successfully navigated the industry you want to be a part of. [ Matteo Wong & Charlie Warzel: AI agents are here. Nobody’s ready. ] You learn resilience: to take blame when no fault is your own, to humble yourself, to take menial tasks seriously, to go overlooked and unthanked. You learn to make judgment calls and not need external validation to know you’ve done a good job. But most of all, being an executive assistant makes you learn people , which is the most valuable skill in almost any industry. Young people need proof that there’s still a ladder left to climb in corporate America, and that if they’re willing to start on the lowest rung, swallow their pride, and be someone’s executive assistant, they can make it to the top. So, long live the human executive assistant. May their days be plenty and may their bosses be pleased with them. And if the bosses can’t be pleased, let them have the satisfaction of yelling at a 20-something, instead of a screen.
